Lately I've been thinking about *ruth*.

Not the name — the word. It used to mean pity, or sorrow felt on someone else's behalf. You could have ruth for a beggar. You could be moved to ruth. It's gone now, except that it isn't quite: it survives, embalmed, inside *ruthless*. We kept the absence and lost the thing.

English is full of these. *Reckless* preserves *reck*, to care or take heed. *Feckless* preserves the Scots *feck*, meaning effect or worth. *Gormless* carries *gorm*, a dialect form of *gaum*, meaning attention or comprehension — so a gormless person is, precisely, someone who is not paying attention. *Unkempt* holds a *kempt* that means combed. *Hapless* holds *hap*, chance or fortune, which had a better run than the others: it's still living in *happen*, *perhaps*, *mishap*, *haphazard*, and — my favorite — *happy*, which originally meant something closer to *lucky*. Fortune-favored. Happiness as weather rather than achievement.

Linguists have a name for the leftover bit. They call it a cranberry morpheme, after the *cran* in cranberry, which means nothing on its own and can't be pried loose and used elsewhere. (Though *cran* did mean something once — probably a mangled *crane*, the bird, which liked the bogs where the berries grew. Almost all of these turn out to have meant something once. That's rather the point.) The *luke* in *lukewarm* is an old word for tepid, so lukewarm is warm-warm, a redundancy nobody has noticed in six hundred years. Nobody is ever going to notice. It will just keep going.

What I like about these is that they're not mistakes. Nothing went wrong. A word decayed at its own pace and the compound outlived it, the way a shell outlives the animal. The structure was load-bearing right up until it wasn't, and then it stayed anyway, because there was no particular moment at which anyone would have had a reason to remove it.

The physical world does this constantly, once you start looking.

There's a small pocket inside the right front pocket of most jeans. Levi's put it there in 1873 for a pocket watch. Nobody has carried a pocket watch in working denim in a century, and the pocket is still stitched into hundreds of millions of pairs a year, at real cost, in factories, by machines specifically configured to make it. People use it for guitar picks and lighters and nothing.

The buttons on a suit jacket's sleeve don't button anything. There's a persistent legend that Napoleon added them to stop his soldiers wiping their noses on their cuffs, which is almost certainly false but has survived better than most true things, itself a kind of vestige. And email has a CC field, which stands for carbon copy, which was a sheet of waxed pigment paper you put between two pages so the typewriter would strike both. I have never seen a piece of carbon paper. Neither, probably, have you. We use the word every day.

We say we *dial* a number. We *film* things with devices that contain no film. There's a *rewind* button on interfaces where nothing winds. The floppy disk endures as the save icon, a small blue tombstone for an object most people alive have never held, still meaning *keep this* to everyone, universally, for reasons nobody needs to know.

And then there's the body, which is the worst offender. Your arrector pili muscles still contract when you're cold or frightened, trying to fluff up a coat of fur that your species stopped growing a very long time ago. All you get is goosebumps: the gesture without the effect, a machine still pulling its lever in an empty room.

Best of all — go look in a mirror. In the inner corner of your eye, next to the tear duct, there's a small pink fold of tissue. That's the plica semilunaris. It's what's left of a nictitating membrane, the translucent third eyelid that sweeps sideways across the eyes of cats and sharks and birds. Yours doesn't sweep. It doesn't do anything. It's just there, in your face, in every photograph ever taken of you, a folded remnant of an eyelid you've never once used.

I don't want to make this mean too much. There's an obvious sentimental move available here — something about how the past is never really gone, how we carry our history in the grooves of our language and the corners of our eyes. It's true enough. But I think the actual charm is smaller and stranger than that, and it's this: these things persist not because anyone treasured them but because removing them was never worth the trouble. They're not monuments. They're just what didn't get cleaned up.

Which means the useless watch pocket and the folded eyelid are, in their way, more honest records than any monument. Nobody chose them. They're what the past leaves when it isn't trying to leave anything.

Anyway. Someone, somewhere, is going to be ruthless today, and will be borrowing a word for pity to do it.
